reading: The same new cable put into walls of two kinds of house, on the same route in each: in at the top near the right side, across just under the top of the wall, down near the left corner, to a socket near the floor. Most new US homes, timber frame: pulled through holes bored in the studs and down inside one stud bay, behind the board; quick. Most German homes, one plastered brick wall done two ways; a patch of broken plaster at a lower corner shows the brick beneath. Repainted: a duct screwed onto the surface along the route and painted over; quick, but the old wall is unchanged and the duct stays on show. Renovated: a channel cut along the route, the cable laid and plastered over; slow, and the channel stays as a scar.
sourceNote: No numbers are drawn; no hours or days are given. The route follows the installation zones for concealed cables in DIN 18015-3 (BAUNETZ-DIN18015): horizontal runs in the upper zone, 15 to 45 cm below the ceiling; vertical runs in zones 10 to 30 cm beside corners; the socket about 30 cm above the floor. The walls are not drawn to scale. The labels describe general building practice for timber stud walls (cables through holes bored in the studs) and plastered solid brick walls; the analogy is the owner's (transcript 2026-11-16-020) and the plan's analogy dictionary (plan-restart.md, rows 'Timber frame', 'Brick', 'Fresh paint on the facade': paint is a new part put on the old wall while the wall stays as it was). 'Most new US homes' / 'most German homes' are the owner's framing of the analogy, to be backed by the construction sources the plan names for section 0.
